slides.0.title: Winemaking and terroir in depth
slides.0.subtitle: Blending, carbonic maceration, oxidative sweet wines and sparkling
slides.1.title: The logic of blending
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Rules are the recipe
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Languedoc AOC red: principal varieties at least 50%, Mourvèdre plus Syrah at least 20%, Carignan and Cinsaut capped at 40% each; Pic Saint-Loup needs at least 50% Syrah; Fitou at least 40% Carignan; each appellation fixes style through proportions
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Yield limits
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Languedoc AOC base 50 (red) / 54 (rosé) / 60 (white) hL/ha; Terrasses du Larzac 45; Maury 30; Pic Saint-Loup 50 (butoir 60)
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Actual below the cap
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Larzac's actual average is about 30–35 hL/ha, below the 45 cap (Wine With Seth): the cap is not the reality
slides.1.content: Proportion rules, yield and style are three things locked together.
slides.2.title: Carignan and maceration strategy
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Carbonic maceration
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Whole bunches fermented in a CO2-rich environment give softer tannins and fresher wine, a defining Languedoc approach (Wine With Seth)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: The contrast
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Priorat and Roussillon more often destem and macerate longer (Wine With Seth): one variety, two routes
slides.2.highlights.2.title: A source tension
slides.2.highlights.2.content: The same page says carbonic maceration softens acidity in one place and that high acid runs through all quality expressions in another, so we do not state acid reduction as a conclusion
slides.2.content: In an exam write "softens tannin" and avoid the unproven acidity claim.
slides.3.title: Oxidative sweet wines
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Sun and bonbonnes
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Maury often starts ageing in 25-litre glass bonbonnes with summer sun producing rancio, while recent vintage styles are bottled early to keep fruit (Wikipedia)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Rivesaltes styles
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Ambré and Tuilé at least 2 years oxidative ageing; Grenat at least 12 months; Hors d'âge 5 years (Wikipedia)
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Timing of mutage
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Timing of mutage decides residual sugar: the earlier the spirit goes in, the sweeter the wine (a general rule); sources do not fully agree on when spirit is added at Maury, so we do not compare them
slides.3.content: Oxidation here is a flavour goal, not a fault.
slides.4.title: A terroir comparison
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Schist
slides.4.highlights.0.content: Faugères and northern Saint-Chinian: deep colour and maquis aromas; schist holds up to a third of its volume in water (Wikipedia)
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Cool nights
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Terrasses du Larzac summer day-night swings can exceed 20°C; Pic Saint-Loup is cool and wet with about 900–1,000 mm of rain (Wine With Seth)
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Sea breezes
slides.4.highlights.2.content: La Clape is under 12 km from the sea with the Marin bringing moisture; Picpoul de Pinet sits by the Thau lagoon (a style generalisation: high acid and salinity)
slides.4.content: Linking each appellation to a "why" is the heart of tasting-based writing.
